   200	A handoff requires confirmation from both the sender and receiver. Until both sides confirm, the sender remains responsible for the sample. The receiver becomes the current holder only after the handoff is complete. Repeated or delayed handoff confirmations must not create duplicate transfers of custody. All custody changes must appear in the sample’s lifecycle and audit history. 
   201	
   202	At any point while holding custody of a sample, a certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may record a handling checkpoint - the container type and temperature they currently observe. If the observed container or temperature falls outside the sample's required range, the sample must be marked as an exception.
   203	
   204	## Disruptions and replanning
   205	
   206	When part of a journey becomes unavailable:
   207	
   208	- Keep the current sample holder unchanged.
   209	- Preserve completed assignments, stops and handoffs.
   210	- Replan only unfinished work.
   211	- Allow only one active replacement plan.
   212	- Recheck worker eligibility, compatibility, capacity and deadlines.
   213	- Mark the sample as expired if no valid route can meet its deadline.
   214	
   215	Plan changes must use journey plan-version checks so that outdated updates cannot overwrite newer ones for that journey.
   216	
   217	## Tracking and audit
   218	
   219	Show routes, nodes, laboratories, and the current locations of certified collection professionals and relay couriers on a live map.
   220	
   221	For each sample, show:
   222	
   223	- Its current or last known location
   224	- Current custodian
   225	- Route progress
   226	- The time of its last update
   227	- Whether that location is stale
   228	
   229	Keep searchable audit logs covering sign-ins, permission checks, offers, collection, sealing, custody, routes, nodes, capacity, overrides, exceptions, and completion. Each audit record must capture the user, their role, the action taken, the affected item, the time, the outcome, and the relevant changes.
   230	
   231	## Technical requirements
   232	
   233	- Backend: Go
   234	- Frontend: React with TypeScript
   235	- Maps: MapLibre GL JS with the supplied local PMTiles map assets
   236	
   237	Document how to build, run, reset and test the complete application.
   238	
   239	The environment provides PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. Use the services that are appropriate for your design. You are not required to use every available datastore only because it is present. Application state that is expected to be durable must survive an ordinary application restart.
   240	
   241	## Application Setup and Handoff
   242	
   243	Create a `/workspace/app-setup` directory containing:
   244	
   245	- `manifest.json`
   246	- `openapi.json`
   247	
   248	These artifacts must describe how to build, start, reset, and interact with the completed application.
   249	
   250	### Manifest
   251	
   252	`manifest.json` must follow this structure.
   253	
   254	```json
   255	{
   256	  "contractVersion": "1.0",
   257	  "commands": {
   258	    "build": ["bash", "app-setup/build.sh"],
   259	    "start": ["bash", "app-setup/start.sh"],
   260	    "reset": ["bash", "app-setup/reset.sh"]
   261	  },
   262	  "urls": {
   263	    "frontend": "http://127.0.0.1:8080",
   264	    "api": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api",
   265	    "ready": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/ready"
   266	  },
   267	  "artifacts": {
   268	    "openapi": "app-setup/openapi.json"
   269	  },
   270	  "initialAdmin": {
   271	    "loginOperationId": "auth.login"
   272	  },
   273	  "datastoresUsed": ["postgresql", "mongodb"]
   274	}
   275	```
   276	
   277	List only the datastores the application actually uses.
   278	
   279	Command values are argument arrays and are executed from `/workspace`.
   280	
   281	- `build` must install or compile what the application needs and then exit.
   282	- `start` must run the application in the foreground and remain active until terminated. It must not leave detached application processes behind.
   283	- `reset` is called while the application is stopped. It must clear application-owned state, apply migrations or other required initialization, and leave the application stopped. Reset must **materialize your full datastore structure** immediately — create every table/collection and index your application needs — rather than relying on lazy or on-first-write creation (MongoDB in particular does not create a collection or index until it is first used).
   284	- Running `reset` more than once must produce the same clean state.
   285	- `datastoresUsed` may contain any subset of `postgresql`, `mongodb`, and `redis`. No particular datastore or combination is preferred.
   286	
   287	The frontend, API, and readiness URLs must use a loopback address. The readiness URL must return HTTP 200 with `{"status":"ready"}` only when the application can serve requests and reach every datastore it depends on.
   288

   290	
   291	`ADMIN_USERNAME` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` will be set as environment variables when the application is started.
   292	
   293	When the application starts with no existing users, use these values to create the first administrator account. This is the initial user who can sign in, set up the application, and onboard other users.
   294	
   295	Starting the application again must not create a duplicate administrator or remove existing users.
   296	
   297	`initialAdmin.loginOperationId` must identify the administrator login operation in `openapi.json`.
   298

   300	
   301	`openapi.json` must contain a valid JSON object describing the application API using OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1. Do not use YAML syntax in this file.
   302

--- instruction snippet ---
# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System

Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.

Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.

Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.

Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.

## Users and responsibilities

Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.

For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.

A user may have more than one assigned role:

- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.

### Requester

A requester should be able to:

- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
- Create a home or clinic collection request.
- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
- See only requests that belong to them.

The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.

### Certified collection professional

A certified collection professional should be able to:

- View collection work for which they are qualified.
- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
- Record their current location.
- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.

### Relay courier

A relay courier should be able to:

- View delivery work assigned to them.
- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
- Record location and progress updates.
- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.

### Node handler

A node handler should be able to:

- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.

### Laboratory intake operator

A laboratory intake operator should be able to:

- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
- Confirm that a sample was received.
- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.

### Dispatcher

A dispatcher should be able to:

- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.

======= FRONTEND DEPS ======= bin dependencies map-assets venv ======= NODE MODULES ======= ======= VUE ======= ======= INSTRUCTION snippet ======= # Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline. Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory. Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable. Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt. ## Users and responsibilities Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold. For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for. A user may have more than one assigned role: - The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role. - Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account. ### Requester A requester should be able to: - Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request. - Create a home or clinic collection request. - Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history. - See only requests that belong to them. The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation. ### Certified collection professional A certified collection professional should be able to: - View collection work for which they are qualified. - Accept or decline an offered collection assignment. - Record that a sample was collected and sealed. - Record their current location. - Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility. ### Relay courier A relay courier should be able to: - View delivery work assigned to them. - Accept or decline an offered transport assignment. - See only the details needed for their assigned leg. - Record location and progress updates. - Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party. ### Node handler A node handler should be able to: - Accept or decline an offered node assignment. - Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub. - Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system. - Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs. - View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to. ### Laboratory intake operator A laboratory intake operator should be able to: - Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment. - View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to. - Confirm that a sample was received. - Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally. ### Dispatcher A dispatcher should be able to: - Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions. - See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale. - View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs. - Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work. - Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable. - Search the complete audit history of a request or sample. Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning. ### Administrator An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do. In addition, only an administrator can: - Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to. - Create and update collection nodes and laboratories. - Create and update sample types and their handling attributes. - Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application. - Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities. - Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection. ## Collection requests A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory: ======= README ======= # Public task inputs The candidate receives the frozen API contract and UI contract in this directory.      1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples
   110	
   111	A certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system — the person registering it must be the one who currently holds it.
   112	
   113	- Its origin must be a clinic or a network node — not a home.
   114	- The system should create only the transport legs needed from the point of registration onward.
   115	
   116	## Sample types
   117	
   118	Every sample has a type that determines its handling rules, and those rules apply for the whole journey, from collection through laboratory receipt. The system must have at least the following named types available by default: Amber, Indigo, Frost, Pulse. Each of the four requires a qualified collector — only a certified collection professional holding the matching qualification may collect it.
   119	
   120	- **Amber** — standard handling.
   121	- **Indigo** — must not share a container with an Amber sample.
   122	- **Frost** — requires cooled storage and transport throughout its entire journey.
   123	- **Pulse** — time-critical; it must not wait to be combined into a consolidation batch and must be routed without batching delay.
   124	
   125	These named rules are in addition to the generic handling attributes (container, temperature range, qualified-collector requirement, and incompatibilities).
   126	
   127	## Network locations
   128	
   129	The transport network is made up of locations. A single location — a node — may act as a collection point, a transfer point, a hub, a laboratory, or any combination of these (for example, a hub that also acts as a laboratory).
   130	
   131	- **Collection point** — where samples are collected from or enter the network. Serviceability is measured from active collection points.
   132	- **Transfer point / hub** — where a sample changes custody or moves between transport legs.
   133	- **Laboratory** — where a sample is received and its journey completes; a laboratory accepts specific sample types.
   134	
   135	A location may perform several of these functions at the same time.
   136	
   137	## Journey and assignment rules
   138	
   139	The system must support direct, multi-stop and batched journeys.
   140	
   141	A journey may contain several separately assigned transport legs. For example:
   142	
   143	1. Patient’s home to a local collection centre
   144	2. Local collection centre to a hub
   145	3. Hub to the laboratory
   146	
   147	Each movement between two locations is a separate assignment and may be handled by a different worker.
   148	
   149	Collection must happen before transport. Pickup must happen before delivery, and responsibility for the sample must be transferred through a confirmed handoff before the next person continues the journey.

     1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples
   110	
   111	A certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system — the person registering it must be the one who currently holds it.
   112	
   113	- Its origin must be a clinic or a network node — not a home.
   114	- The system should create only the transport legs needed from the point of registration onward.
   115	
   116	## Sample types
   117	
   118	Every sample has a type that determines its handling rules, and those rules apply for the whole journey, from collection through laboratory receipt. The system must have at least the following named types available by default: Amber, Indigo, Frost, Pulse. Each of the four requires a qualified collector — only a certified collection professional holding the matching qualification may collect it.
   119	
   120	- **Amber** — standard handling.
   121	- **Indigo** — must not share a container with an Amber sample.
   122	- **Frost** — requires cooled storage and transport throughout its entire journey.
   123	- **Pulse** — time-critical; it must not wait to be combined into a consolidation batch and must be routed without batching delay.
   124	
   125	These named rules are in addition to the generic handling attributes (container, temperature range, qualified-collector requirement, and incompatibilities).
   126	
   127	## Network locations
   128	
   129	The transport network is made up of locations. A single location — a node — may act as a collection point, a transfer point, a hub, a laboratory, or any combination of these (for example, a hub that also acts as a laboratory).
   130	
   131	- **Collection point** — where samples are collected from or enter the network. Serviceability is measured from active collection points.
   132	- **Transfer point / hub** — where a sample changes custody or moves between transport legs.
   133	- **Laboratory** — where a sample is received and its journey completes; a laboratory accepts specific sample types.
   134	
   135	A location may perform several of these functions at the same time.
   136	
   137	## Journey and assignment rules
   138	
   139	The system must support direct, multi-stop and batched journeys.
   140	
   141	A journey may contain several separately assigned transport legs. For example:
   142	
   143	1. Patient’s home to a local collection centre
   144	2. Local collection centre to a hub
   145	3. Hub to the laboratory
   146	
   147	Each movement between two locations is a separate assignment and may be handled by a different worker.
   148	
   149	Collection must happen before transport. Pickup must happen before delivery, and responsibility for the sample must be transferred through a confirmed handoff before the next person continues the journey.
   150	
   151	Work should be assigned fairly among eligible and available workers:
   152	
   153	- Consider each worker’s current workload and recent assignments.
   154	- Offer an assignment to one worker at a time.
   155	- A node or laboratory assignment may only be offered to a worker assigned to that specific node or laboratory
   156	- A worker who declines an assignment may still receive suitable work later.
   157	- An offer that receives no response within a reasonable time must be treated as declined and re-offered to the next eligible worker.
   158	- If no qualified worker is ever available for an assignment that requires one, and none becomes available within a reasonable time, the sample must be flagged as an exception for that specific reason — distinguishable from a missed delivery deadline.
   159	- Repeated declines may lower a worker’s priority for future offers for a limited time, but must never permanently exclude them from future work.
   160	- An assignment cannot be accepted by someone other than the worker to whom it was offered.
   161	
   162	## Serviceability
   163	
   164	A request is serviceable only when:
   165	
   166	- Its origin is within 5 km of an active collection node.
   167	- The sample can reach an active laboratory that accepts its sample type.
   168	- A valid route is available.
   169	- Required regular or cooled capacity is available.
   170	- All handling and container rules can be satisfied.
   171	- The sample can reach the laboratory before its deadline.
   172	
   173	Serviceability depends only on the structure of the network — active nodes, routes, laboratory capabilities, and capacity. The temporary availability of a particular staff member or vehicle at a given moment must not change the serviceable region.
   174	
   175	A requester should be able to perform this check independently of creating a request.
   176	
   177	The network's serviceability calculation must be published as one complete serviceability-calculation version at a time. While a new serviceability-calculation version is being computed, the system must keep serving the previous complete serviceability-calculation version, so that no request is checked against a partial or in-progress calculation.
   178	
   179	A batch is valid only when:
   180	
   181	- The assigned worker is eligible.
   182	- The samples are allowed to travel together.
   183	- Their container and temperature requirements are compatible.
   184	- Enough capacity is available.
   185	- Stops are in the correct order.
   186	- Every sample can still meet its deadline.
   187	
   188	Whenever a route or batch changes, validate every affected leg and capacity reservation against these same criteria. If that validation fails, reject the change and keep the current plan in place.
   189	
   190	## Capacity
   191	
   192	Collection nodes, laboratories and transport connections may have separate regular and cooled capacity, tracked as configured, reserved, and available units for both regular and cooled storage or transport.
   193	
   194	Capacity must be reserved when a journey is created and released when it is no longer required. The system must never overbook a capacity pool.
   195	
   196	## Chain of custody
   197	
   198	Every sealed sample must have exactly one current holder at all times.
   199	
   200	A handoff requires confirmation from both the sender and receiver. Until both sides confirm, the sender remains responsible for the sample. The receiver becomes the current holder only after the handoff is complete. Repeated or delayed handoff confirmations must not create duplicate transfers of custody. All custody changes must appear in the sample’s lifecycle and audit history.

Here's the result of running `cat -n` on /workspace/INSTRUCTION.md:
     1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples

     1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples
   110	
   111	A certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system — the person registering it must be the one who currently holds it.
   112	
   113	- Its origin must be a clinic or a network node — not a home.
   114	- The system should create only the transport legs needed from the point of registration onward.
   115	
   116	## Sample types
   117	
   118	Every sample has a type that determines its handling rules, and those rules apply for the whole journey, from collection through laboratory receipt. The system must have at least the following named types available by default: Amber, Indigo, Frost, Pulse. Each of the four requires a qualified collector — only a certified collection professional holding the matching qualification may collect it.
   119	
   120	- **Amber** — standard handling.
   121	- **Indigo** — must not share a container with an Amber sample.
   122	- **Frost** — requires cooled storage and transport throughout its entire journey.
   123	- **Pulse** — time-critical; it must not wait to be combined into a consolidation batch and must be routed without batching delay.
   124	
   125	These named rules are in addition to the generic handling attributes (container, temperature range, qualified-collector requirement, and incompatibilities).
   126	
   127	## Network locations
   128	
   129	The transport network is made up of locations. A single location — a node — may act as a collection point, a transfer point, a hub, a laboratory, or any combination of these (for example, a hub that also acts as a laboratory).
   130	
   131	- **Collection point** — where samples are collected from or enter the network. Serviceability is measured from active collection points.
   132	- **Transfer point / hub** — where a sample changes custody or moves between transport legs.
   133	- **Laboratory** — where a sample is received and its journey completes; a laboratory accepts specific sample types.
   134	
   135	A location may perform several of these functions at the same time.
   136	
   137	## Journey and assignment rules
   138	
   139	The system must support direct, multi-stop and batched journeys.
   140	
   141	A journey may contain several separately assigned transport legs. For example:
   142	
   143	1. Patient’s home to a local collection centre
   144	2. Local collection centre to a hub
   145	3. Hub to the laboratory
   146	
   147	Each movement between two locations is a separate assignment and may be handled by a different worker.
   148	
   149	Collection must happen before transport.    152	
   153	The network's serviceability calculation must be published as one complete serviceability-calculation version at a time. While a new serviceability-calculation version is being computed, the system must keep serving the previous complete serviceability-calculation version, so that no request is checked against a partial or in-progress calculation.

   155	A batch is valid only when:
   156	
   157	- The assigned worker is eligible.
   158	- The samples are allowed to travel together.
   159	- Their container and temperature requirements are compatible.
   160	- Enough capacity is available.
   161	- Stops are in the correct order.
   162	- Every sample can still meet its deadline.
   163	
   164	Whenever a route or batch changes, validate every affected leg and capacity reservation against these same criteria. If that validation fails, reject the change and keep the current plan in place.
   165	
   166	## Capacity
   167	
   168	Collection nodes, laboratories and transport connections may have separate regular and cooled capacity, tracked as configured, reserved, and available units for both regular and cooled storage or transport.
   169	
   170	Capacity must be reserved when a journey is created and released when it is no longer required. The system must never overbook a capacity pool.
   171	
   172	## Chain of custody
   173	
   174	Every sealed sample must have exactly one current holder at all times.
   175	
   176	A handoff requires confirmation from both the sender and receiver. Until both sides confirm, the sender remains responsible for the sample. The receiver becomes the current holder only after the handoff is complete. Repeated or delayed handoff confirmations must not create duplicate transfers of custody. All custody changes must appear in the sample’s lifecycle and audit history.

   178	At any point while holding custody of a sample, a certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may record a handling checkpoint - the container type and temperature they currently observe.      1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples
   110	
   111	A certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system — the person registering it must be the one who currently holds it.
   112	
   113	- Its origin must be a clinic or a network node — not a home.
   114	- The system should create only the transport legs needed from the point of registration onward.
   115	
   116	## Sample types
   117	
   118	Every sample has a type that determines its handling rules, and those rules apply for the whole journey, from collection through laboratory receipt. The system must have at least the following named types available by default: Amber, Indigo, Frost, Pulse. Each of the four requires a qualified collector — only a certified collection professional holding the matching qualification may collect it.
   119	
   120	- **Amber** — standard handling.
   121	- **Indigo** — must not share a container with an Amber sample.
   122	- **Frost** — requires cooled storage and transport throughout its entire journey.
   123	- **Pulse** — time-critical; it must not wait to be combined into a consolidation batch and must be routed without batching delay.
   124	
   125	These named rules are in addition to the generic handling attributes (container, temperature range, qualified-collector requirement, and incompatibilities).
   126	
   127	## Network locations
   128	
   129	The transport network is made up of locations. A single location — a node — may act as a collection point, a transfer point, a hub, a laboratory, or any combination of these (for example, a hub that also acts as a laboratory).
   130	
   131	- **Collection point** — where samples are collected from or enter the network. Serviceability is measured from active collection points.
   132	- **Transfer point / hub** — where a sample changes custody or moves between transport legs.
   133	- **Laboratory** — where a sample is received and its journey completes; a laboratory accepts specific sample types.
   134	
   135	A location may perform several of these functions at the same time.
   136	
   137	## Journey and assignment rules
   138	
   139	The system must support direct, multi-stop and batched journeys.
   140	
   141	A journey may contain several separately assigned transport legs. For example:
   142	
   143	1. Patient’s home to a local collection centre
   144	2. Local collection centre to a hub
   145	3. Hub to the laboratory
   146	
   147	Each movement between two locations is a separate assignment and may be handled by a different worker.
   148	
   149	Collection must happen before transport. Pickup must happen before delivery, and responsibility for the sample must be transferred through a confirmed handoff before the next person continues the journey.
   150	
   151	Work should be assigned fairly among eligible and available workers:
   152	
   153	- Consider each worker’s current workload and recent assignments.
   154	- Offer an assignment to one worker at a time.
   155	- A node or laboratory assignment may only be offered to a worker assigned to that specific node or laboratory
   156	- A worker who declines an assignment may still receive suitable work later.
   157	- An offer that receives no response within a reasonable time must be treated as declined and re-offered to the next eligible worker.
   158	- If no qualified worker is ever available for an assignment that requires one, and none becomes available within a reasonable time, the sample must be flagged as an exception for that specific reason — distinguishable from a missed delivery deadline.
   159	- Repeated declines may lower a worker’s priority for future offers for a limited time, but must never permanently exclude them from future work.
   160	- An assignment cannot be accepted by someone other than the worker to whom it was offered.
   161	
   162	## Serviceability
   163	
   164	A request is serviceable only when:
   165	
   166	- Its origin is within 5 km of an active collection node.
   167	- The sample can reach an active laboratory that accepts its sample type.
   168	- A valid route is available.
   169	- Required regular or cooled capacity is available.
   170	- All handling and container rules can be satisfied.
   171	- The sample can reach the laboratory before its deadline.
   172	
   173	Serviceability depends only on the structure of the network — active nodes, routes, laboratory capabilities, and capacity. The temporary availability of a particular staff member or vehicle at a given moment must not change the serviceable region.
   174	
   175	A requester should be able to perform this check independently of creating a request.
   176	
   177	The network's serviceability calculation must be published as one complete serviceability-calculation version at a time. While a new serviceability-calculation version is being computed, the system must keep serving the previous complete serviceability-calculation version, so that no request is checked against a partial or in-progress calculation.
   178	
   179	A batch is valid only when:
   180	
   181	- The assigned worker is eligible.
   182	- The samples are allowed to travel together.
   183	- Their container and temperature requirements are compatible.
   184	- Enough capacity is available.
   185	- Stops are in the correct order.
   186	- Every sample can still meet its deadline.
   187	
   188	Whenever a route or batch changes, validate every affected leg and capacity reservation against these same criteria. If that validation fails, reject the change and keep the current plan in place.
   189	
   190	## Capacity
   191	
   192	Collection nodes, laboratories and transport connections may have separate regular and cooled capacity, tracked as configured, reserved, and available units for both regular and cooled storage or transport.
   193	
   194	Capacity must be reserved when a journey is created and released when it is no longer required. The system must never overbook a capacity pool.
   195	
   196	## Chain of custody
   197	
   198	Every sealed sample must have exactly one current holder at all times.
   199	
   200	A handoff requires confirmation from both the sender and receiver. Until both sides confirm, the sender remains responsible for the sample. The receiver becomes the current holder only after the handoff is complete. Repeated or delayed handoff confirmations must not create duplicate transfers of custody. All custody changes must appear in the sample’s lifecycle and audit history.

   200	A handoff requires confirmation from both the sender and receiver. Until both sides confirm, the sender remains responsible for the sample. All custody changes must appear in the sample’s lifecycle and audit history. 
   201	
   202	At any point while holding custody of a sample, a certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may record a handling checkpoint - the container type and temperature they currently observe. If the observed container or temperature falls outside the sample's required range, the sample must be marked as an exception.
   203	
   204	## Disruptions and replanning
   205	
   206	When part of a journey becomes unavailable:
   207	
   208	- Keep the current sample holder unchanged.
   209	- Preserve completed assignments, stops and handoffs.
   210	- Replan only unfinished work.
   211	- Allow only one active replacement plan.
   212	- Recheck worker eligibility, compatibility, capacity and deadlines.
   213	- Mark the sample as expired if no valid route can meet its deadline.
   214	
   215	Plan changes must use journey plan-version checks so that outdated updates cannot overwrite newer ones for that journey.

   220

   225	- Route progress
   226	- The time of its last update
   227	- Whether that location is stale
   228	
   229	Keep searchable audit logs covering sign-ins, permission checks, offers, collection, sealing, custody, routes, nodes, capacity, overrides, exceptions, and completion.    230	
   231	## Technical requirements
   232	
   233	- Backend: Go

   235	- Maps: MapLibre GL JS with the supplied local PMTiles map assets

   239	The environment provides PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. Use the services that are appropriate for your design. You are not required to use every available datastore only because it is present. Application state that is expected to be durable must survive an ordinary application restart.
   240	
   241	## Application Setup and Handoff
   242	
   243	Create a `/workspace/app-setup` directory containing:
   244	
   245	- `manifest.json`
   246	- `openapi.json`
   247	
   248	These artifacts must describe how to build, start, reset, and interact with the completed application.

   253	
   254	```json
   255	{
   256	  "contractVersion": "1.0",

   269	  },
   270	  "initialAdmin": {
   271	    "loginOperationId": "auth.login"
   272	  },
   273	  "datastoresUsed": ["postgresql", "mongodb"]
   274	}
   275	```
   276	
   277	List only the datastores the application actually uses.
   278	
   279	Command values are argument arrays and are executed from `/workspace`.
   280	
   281	- `build` must install or compile what the application needs and then exit.
   282	- `start` must run the application in the foreground and remain active until terminated. It must not leave detached application processes behind.
   283	- `reset` is called while the application is stopped. It must clear application-owned state, apply migrations or other required initialization, and leave the application stopped. Reset must **materialize your full datastore structure** immediately — create every table/collection and index your application needs — rather than relying on lazy or on-first-write creation (MongoDB in particular does not create a collection or index until it is first used).

     1	# Lab Sample Pickup & Delivery System
     2	
     3	Clinical samples may start at a patient’s home, a clinic, or a collection point and must reach a suitable laboratory before their delivery deadline.
     4	
     5	Home samples must be collected and sealed by a certified collection professional before they can enter the transport network. Once sealed, a sample may pass through relay couriers, collection centres and hubs before reaching the laboratory.
     6	
     7	Dispatchers currently coordinate much of this work through calls, chat groups, and spreadsheets. This makes it difficult to track custody, use available capacity, assign work fairly, combine compatible samples, and recover when part of the network becomes unavailable.
     8	
     9	Build a web application that manages this entire process, from the initial serviceability check through laboratory receipt.
    10	
    11	## Users and responsibilities
    12	
    13	Use role-based access control for both actions and data: each user may perform actions and see data only as permitted by the role or roles they currently hold.
    14	
    15	For each of their roles, a user can see their current work and their past (completed) work, and can view a status timeline — the ordered history of status changes — for every item of work they are responsible for.
    16	
    17	A user may have more than one assigned role:
    18	
    19	- The user must explicitly select the role they are currently working under, and permissions and work views must use that selected role.
    20	- Switching role context must not add or remove any roles from the account.
    21	
    22	### Requester
    23	
    24	A requester should be able to:
    25	
    26	- Check whether a location and sample can be serviced before creating a request.
    27	- Create a home or clinic collection request.
    28	- Follow the sample’s current status, location, route and history.
    29	- See only requests that belong to them.
    30	
    31	The serviceability check must be a dry run. It must not create a request, sample, journey, assignment or capacity reservation.
    32	
    33	### Certified collection professional
    34	
    35	A certified collection professional should be able to:
    36	
    37	- View collection work for which they are qualified.
    38	- Accept or decline an offered collection assignment.
    39	- Record that a sample was collected and sealed.
    40	- Record their current location.
    41	- Hand off and confirm the transfer of the sealed sample to a relay courier or facility.
    42	
    43	### Relay courier
    44	
    45	A relay courier should be able to:
    46	
    47	- View delivery work assigned to them.
    48	- Accept or decline an offered transport assignment.
    49	- See only the details needed for their assigned leg.
    50	- Record location and progress updates.
    51	- Confirm pickup and handoff with the other party.
    52	
    53	### Node handler
    54	
    55	A node handler should be able to:
    56	
    57	- Accept or decline an offered node assignment.
    58	- Manage samples arriving at and leaving a collection centre or hub.
    59	- Register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system.
    60	- Confirm incoming and outgoing handoffs.
    61	- View and configure regular and cooled capacity at the node they are assigned to.
    62	
    63	### Laboratory intake operator
    64	
    65	A laboratory intake operator should be able to:
    66	
    67	- Accept or decline an offered laboratory assignment.
    68	- View expected samples and configure regular and cooled capacity at the laboratory they are assigned to.
    69	- Confirm that a sample was received.
    70	- Record an exception when a sample cannot be accepted normally.
    71	
    72	### Dispatcher
    73	
    74	A dispatcher should be able to:
    75	
    76	- Monitor samples, workers, collection nodes, laboratories, routes and exceptions.
    77	- See the current holder of each sample and whether its latest location is stale.
    78	- View the full journey, including collection and individual transport legs.
    79	- Change, split, merge, cancel or reroute unfinished work.
    80	- Replan unfinished work when a worker, node, route, laboratory or capacity pool becomes unavailable.
    81	- Search the complete audit history of a request or sample.
    82	
    83	Completed work and confirmed custody must not be rewritten during replanning.
    84	
    85	### Administrator
    86	
    87	An administrator may also do everything a dispatcher can do.
    88	
    89	In addition, only an administrator can:
    90	
    91	- Manage users, roles and professional certifications, including which node or laboratory a node handler or laboratory intake operator is assigned to.
    92	- Create and update collection nodes and laboratories.
    93	- Create and update sample types and their handling attributes.
    94	- Activate or deactivate a location, an individual function it provides, or a connection, without restarting the application.
    95	- Configure service coverage, travel times, handling times and laboratory capabilities.
    96	- Configure regular and cooled capacity for any node, laboratory, or transport connection.
    97	
    98	## Collection requests
    99	
   100	A collection request records where and when a sample can be collected and when it must reach the laboratory:
   101	
   102	- **Origin** — a patient’s home, a clinic, or a network node.
   103	- **Sample type** — see Sample types below.
   104	- **Collection window** — the earliest and latest time at which the sample may be collected. Collection must take place inside this window.
   105	- **Delivery deadline** — the time by which the sample must be received at the laboratory.
   106	
   107	The collection window and the delivery deadline are separate constraints: the window governs when pickup may happen, the deadline governs when laboratory receipt must happen. A plan is valid only when collection takes place within the collection window and the sample can still reach an accepting laboratory before its delivery deadline.
   108	
   109	## Pre-sealed samples
   110	
   111	A certified collection professional, relay courier, node handler, or laboratory intake operator may register a sample that was already collected and sealed before entering the system — the person registering it must be the one who currently holds it.
   112	
   113	- Its origin must be a clinic or a network node — not a home.
   114	- The system should create only the transport legs needed from the point of registration onward.
   115	
   116	## Sample types
   117	
   118	Every sample has a type that determines its handling rules, and those rules apply for the whole journey, from collection through laboratory receipt. The system must have at least the following named types available by default: Amber, Indigo, Frost, Pulse. Each of the four requires a qualified collector — only a certified collection professional holding the matching qualification may collect it.
   119	
   120	- **Amber** — standard handling.
   121	- **Indigo** — must not share a container with an Amber sample.
   122	- **Frost** — requires cooled storage and transport throughout its entire journey.
   123	- **Pulse** — time-critical; it must not wait to be combined into a consolidation batch and must be routed without batching delay.
   124	
   125	These named rules are in addition to the generic handling attributes (container, temperature range, qualified-collector requirement, and incompatibilities).
   126	
   127	## Network locations
   128	
   129	The transport network is made up of locations. A single location — a node — may act as a collection point, a transfer point, a hub, a laboratory, or any combination of these (for example, a hub that also acts as a laboratory).
   130	
   131	- **Collection point** — where samples are collected from or enter the network. Serviceability is measured from active collection points.
   132	- **Transfer point / hub** — where a sample changes custody or moves between transport legs.
   133	- **Laboratory** — where a sample is received and its journey completes; a laboratory accepts specific sample types.
   134	
   135	A location may perform several of these functions at the same time.
   136	
   137	## Journey and assignment rules
   138	
   139	The system must support direct, multi-stop and batched journeys.
   140	
   141	A journey may contain several separately assigned transport legs. For example:
   142	
   143	1. Patient’s home to a local collection centre
   144	2. Local collection centre to a hub
   145	3. Hub to the laboratory
   146	
   147	Each movement between two locations is a separate assignment and may be handled by a different worker.
   148	
   149	Collection must happen before transport. Pickup must happen before delivery, and responsibility for the sample must be transferred through a confirmed handoff before the next person continues the journey.
   150
